newsitem.title: UK: UK regulator irks funds with pension reform call.
newsitem.headline: UK regulator irks funds with pension reform call.

text.p: A British regulator's call for more "passive-style" pension fund management was criticised by fund managers on Tuesday, but a consultant said active managers' performance was not enough to justify the costs.

"Its a sweeping generalisation. I'm surprised at the Office for Fair Trading (OFT) suggesting that we limit consumer choice," said Steven Cameron, director of pensions development at Scottish Equitable.

In a report on the industry, OFT director general John Bridgeman called for radical changes in the way pension funds are managed, including a move away from actively traded portfolios to so-called "index funds", which attempt to replicate the performance of market indices.
"There is no convincing evidence that fund managers can consistently outperform the market over the period of a pension plan although the industry does not like to face up to this," Bridgeman said.
But Julian Samways, head of marketing at Schroder Investment Management, said, "There is evidence that a proportion of active managers do consistently outperform indices."
Samways said that pension funds that choose the outperformers benefit and that performance can last for extended periods.
"The emphasis must be on a good investment manager selection exercise to get the right managers."
But some consultants and fund managers disagreed with Samways.
"On aggregate, active managers don't really produce the sort of returns that are worth paying for," said Alastair MacDougall, of consultants WM Company.

A WM Company study of more than 200 billion stg in UK pension funds showed that between 1986 and 1995 index funds returned 15.1 percent per annum, versus 14.7 percent for actively managed funds. This compares to a 15.2 percent per annum growth in the FTSE-A All-Share index.

And index funds have more consistent returns, according to MacDougall. "There will always be active funds that do spectacularly well but there will always be funds that do particularly badly. The whole point about the index approach is that it gives you a defined return relative to a given index."
The vast majority of UK pension funds use active managers for their equity portfolios with only 15-20 percent of funds managed by index funds, according to WM Company.
But this number has been growing, tracking the spectacular growth of index-linked investment in the U.S., where it has captured about 30 percent of the pension market.

If British pension funds and individual pension plans moved wholesale to index funds there would be a large loss of jobs in the investment management industry, according to Stephen Tanner, director general of the Institutional Fund Mangers Association.

"I wouldn't like to count how many fund managers I've put out of business over the last ten years," said James Woodlock, managing director at Barclays Global Investors, the world's largest passive investment manager.
"The advantages are low cost and certainty," he said.

Passive fund managers charge eight to ten basis points of face value per annum management fee for a 100 million stg equity portfolio, as opposed to 25-30 basis points for an active manager, fund managers said.
But savings are also achieved in lower trading costs, Woodlock said.

Index-linked portfolios, many of which only change as the underlying index does, have far less turnover than active portfolios, with turnover in all index-type funds about 15 percent annually, according to WM Company. This compares to turnover of between 50-80 percent in active portfolios.
But Samways cautions that an over-reliance on index funds can lead to distortions in the market, as the proportion of freely traded shares diminishes.
"You could get a situation where the guy with the one freely traded share of Boots is able to move the market."
